paragraphs: In this passage, we come to what is commonly known as the “Daniel Fast”. Fasting is a consecrated time of total reliance on God. At the heart of fasting is deep soul-work.
Biblical characters modeled fasting for various reasons and for various timespans:
Moses: “I stayed on the mountain forty days and forty nights; I ate no bread and drank no water.” (Deut. 9:9)
David – “David pleaded with God for the child. He fasted and spent the nights lying in sackcloth on the ground.” (2 Sam. 12:16)
Elijah – “Strengthened by that food, he traveled forty days and forty nights until he reached Horeb, the mountain of God.” (1 Kgs. 19:8)
Anna – “She never left the temple but worshiped night and day, fasting and praying.” (Lk. 2:37)
Jesus – “After fasting forty days and forty nights, he was hungry.” (Matt. 4:2)
Paul – “While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting.” (Ac. 13:2)

As a Christian, when was the last time you fasted? For what reason did you fast? Was it to grow in closer intimacy with God? Was it for the healing of a family member? Was it before making an important decision? All of these are valid reasons.

Let us return to the scenario of Daniel, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego and the details of their fast. These four young men resisted assimilation into Babylonian culture by fasting. It was permissible for them to learn the language and read the literature, but it was not beneficial for them to adopt their spirituality by way of eating non-kosher food or food sacrificed to idols. They had drawn a line of demarcation that they wanted to preserve and were unwilling to cross. This is a reminder that we need to live within biblical boundaries. In Daniel 1:12, we read, “Please test your servants for ten days: Give us nothing but vegetables to eat and water to drink.” Notice that this is called a test, although it was a type of fast. They did not do this out of rebellion, but with permission. By stepping out in faith, they were fasting before God, but testing King Nebuchadnezzar on the topic of his sovereignty.

The kings and kingdoms of the earth are systemically trying to assimilate us into patterns of worldliness. In the midst of this, we have a Sovereign God that shows us the pathway of godliness. It may be unpopular, but when put to the test, it yields powerful results. I want to encourage you to consider fasting during these eight weeks in the Book of Daniel. For example, you could fast one meal for seven days (seven-day fast). You could fast one meal from Monday to Friday for the next eight weeks (forty-day fast). There are options so choose your commitment and carry it through to completion. Let the Lord identify the areas in your life where you are assimilating to the dominant culture. It is time to take a stand and make a sacrifice that will lead to spiritual health and strength.
Pastor Chris Padiath

paragraphs: Have you ever awakened from a dream you couldn’t quite remember, but still felt a lingering sense of fear and unease? In Daniel 2, King Nebuchadnezzar was deeply distressed by his dream that he threatened to kill the wise men unless they could accurately describe and interpret it.

Daniel, a captive from Judah, sought to save himself, his friends, and the wise men of the kingdom. He relied solely on God, the author of the dream (Dan. 2:28) and urged his friends to join him in beseeching God in prayer (Dan. 2:18).

Daniel elucidated that the king beheld a remarkable figure with a head of fine gold, chest and arms of silver, torso and thighs of bronze, legs of iron, and feet and toes made of a mixture of iron and clay. Many have speculated that these segments represent the empires of Babylon, Persia, Greece and Rome.

God's desire to communicate with us is evident throughout scripture. Numbers 12:6 and 1 Corinthians 2:9-16 refer to God revealing unknown things to his servants through visions and dreams, while Joel 2:28 prophecies that in the last days, God will pour out His Spirit, prompting both old and young to receive divine revelations through dreams and visions. God desires to impart deep truths that can shape us into Christ's image and influence the world. God invites us into deeper intimacy with Him, where we can bring our most complex questions, knowing He will respond, as He did for Daniel.

Some dreams do not foretell the future; they mirror our current concerns, aspirations or replay past experiences. It is wise to discern dreams prayerfully with wise counsel; disregard some and heed warnings if needed. Nevertheless, every dream demands surrender to God. We replace fear and confusion with confidence with the knowledge of His enduring presence.

The power of intercessory prayer. Daniel requested his friends to pray alongside him. In times of need, do we humbly seek prayer support from our Christian community (Rom. 15:30 & Eph. 6:19) or does pride prevent us from seeking help? Are we facing challenges relying solely on our own  strength? Utilizing the “Prayer Request” feature in the WPA Bible Engagement app exemplifies one way to practice communal prayer and support.

Our understanding of God's deeper truths hinges on how we respond faithfully to the teachings we already know from His Word. Are we like King Nebuchadnezzar who recognized Daniel's God as "the God of gods and a revealer of mysteries," yet later erected a statue of himself and commanded others to worship it as mentioned in Daniel 3? Alternatively, are we like Daniel, persistently pursuing God and witnessing deeper revelations? God unveils profound truths to those who obediently follow the word He has already disclosed.
Prima Fernandes

paragraphs: In Daniel 2, King Nebuchadnezzar first becomes acquainted with the mighty power of God when Daniel not only interprets his dream, but knows the dream without having been told. Daniel shares with Nebuchadnezzar that, "The God of heaven has given you dominion and power and might and glory; in your hands he has placed all mankind and the beasts of the field and the birds in the sky. Wherever they live, he has made you ruler over them all" (Dan. 2:37-38). His response is immediate and appropriate; he falls prostrate before Daniel and says, "Surely your God is the God of gods and the Lord of kings" (Dan. 2:47) and yet, in today’s reading, it seems he has forgotten who God is. He builds a huge statue that he commands everyone to worship on penalty of death. When Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego refuse to worship the statue, Nebuchadnezzar’s fury is unleashed as he exclaims, "What god will be able to rescue you from my hand?" (Dan. 3:15). He has forgotten that his own power was given to him by the God who he had said was "the God of gods and the Lord of kings." Moments later, he witnesses the three Hebrew men protected from certain death and he once again acknowledges God, saying "Praise be to the God of Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego" (Dan. 3:28).

Later, Nebuchadnezzar has another dream. When he calls Daniel once again to interpret it, his reverence for the one true God has become lukewarm at best. He comments, "I know that the spirit of the holy gods is in you" (Dan. 4:9). God has become just "one of the gods" again, no longer "God of gods or Lord of kings".

Daniel explains that the dream is God’s intent on punishing Nebuchadnezzar "until you acknowledge that the Most High is sovereign over all kingdoms on earth" (Dan. 4:25). Although the king had been moved twice before by experiencing God’s power, he had not yet fully surrendered himself and acknowledged God as his Sovereign and Lord.

The king knew the truth about God, but did not act on the truth. He experienced God’s power from time to time, but he did not allow it to transform his heart. It took a dramatic punishment from God for him to finally recognize God’s supreme power and authority and to commit himself to God alone.

Many people, like Nebuchadnezzar, are greatly moved by an encounter with God and yet do not allow it to transform them from the inside out. Their enthusiasm and commitment gradually fizzle out. We need to be people who not only acknowledge God’s power and might, but people who have surrendered completely to God and are allowing Him to reshape us into His likeness, for HIS glory. The prophet Hanani wrote, "For the eyes of the Lord roam throughout the earth, so that He may strongly support those whose heart is completely His" (2 Chron. 16:9). I want to be someone whose heart is completely His, someone He can strongly support. You can be that person too!
John Pellowe

paragraphs: Babylon was a remarkable city in antiquity. Ancient historians, like Herodutus and Josephus, give us a glimpse with details on its grandeur. The city had forty-foot-high, double-encased walls on which two chariots could pass. The city had eight gates, including a double gate dedicated to the goddess Ishtar that led to a three hundred foot ziggurat (pyramid) and the temple of Marduk. Babylon boasted the lush Hanging Gardens, which were built for Nebuchadnezzar’s Median wife, Amytis, to remind her of her homeland. Babylon also had a sophisticated water supply system that supplied its inhabitants with water from the Euphrates through multiple canals. No other city boasted such engineering marvels; Babylon was truly exceptional.

This is the city that King Nebuchadnezzar reflects on from his rooftop terrace. As he gazes upon his accomplishments, he declares: "Is not this the great Babylon I have built as the royal residence, by my mighty power and for the glory of my majesty?" (Dan. 4:30). This prideful outburst is in sharp contrast to the warnings in a dream. Just twelve months earlier, God warned Nebuchadnezzar to rule in light of His sovereignty. Unfortunately, the king of Babylon, bursting with pride, disregarded the warning and found himself experiencing the dread dream. His judgment was swift and for a period of "seven times" (probably seven years), he sank to the level of a beast, living outdoors alongside the wild animals until he looked up and honoured the One who truly is the highest power and sovereign over all things. Nebuchadnezzar’s humility and contrition resulted in healing, which then led to him being restored to the throne and becoming even greater than before.

Daniel 4 is an illustration of many warnings in scripture regarding pride (e.g., Prov. 16:18 & Jm. 4:6). So is all pride a sin? Could we, as a Christian, ever be proud of any of our accomplishments? Are we sinning when we walk across the stage to receive a graduation certificate, purchase our first home or present year-end accomplishments at the company for which we work?

Nebuchadnezzar’s words in verse thirty reveal two important insights about pride. The first is his claim that his own power was the source of these accomplishments. Sinful pride, here, believes that all of this was accomplished entirely in and of himself. God had no part to play in acquiring the skills, conditions and resources to achieve the feat. The second element that makes the king’s pride sinful is the motivation for his building accomplishments. Nebuchadnezzar did it for "the glory of [his] majesty." This was the same pride Lucifer evidenced in Isaiah 14:12-15.  Both of them were hungry for the glory that belonged to the Lord.

From this, we should recognize that only God is worthy of worship because He alone is able to accomplish things entirely in and of Himself. God is holy, beautiful, glorious and powerful in and of Himself. Everything and everyone (including us) relies on God, whether we realize it or not. So it isn’t a matter of not being proud of our accomplishments, but a matter of directing worship in the proper direction. As James 1:17 points out, "Every good and perfect gift is from above." This means that we need to walk humbly, even in light of any meaningful accomplishment we may achieve. In our lives, we recognize that God is the source of every good thing. Often, a good way to gauge pride in our hearts is in how we talk about our accomplishments? How are you doing with pride? Is there something for which you need to redirect credit to God?
Pastor Daniel Weigert

paragraphs: A decree had been issued by King Darius. No one was to pray or call upon any deity or human being except the king for thirty days. A group of high-ranking officials who were jealous of Daniel had connived and successfully convinced the king to issue this decree.
Daniel went up to his house to pray, three times a day, his windows open towards Jerusalem, as was his custom since early days. This could seem like a wreckless move by Daniel.

In Daniel 2:17-19, when the king would have executed all the wise men in his realm for their inability to interpret his dream, "Daniel went to his house, and made the decision known to Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, his companions, that they might seek mercies from the God of heaven concerning this secret [PRAYED], so that Daniel and his companions might not perish with the rest of the wise men of Babylon. Then the secret was revealed to Daniel in a night vision. So Daniel blessed the God of heaven". This account confirms that, in the place of prayer, revelations are given. In the place of prayer, decrees are brought to nothing!

For Daniel, prayer was a habit and lifestyle. In today’s text we note that three times a day he got down on his knees and prayed, giving thanks to his God just as he had done before. This was his custom, his lifestyle in spite of the high office he occupied.

Long before Paul’s charge to the Ephesian church to "pray always with all kinds of prayer" (Eph. 6:18), Daniel was living that out in the Old Testament. Daniel’s prayer lifestyle also reminds me of our Lord Jesus Christ in His earthly life, of whom the scripture said, "Now in the morning, having risen a long while before daylight, He went out and departed to a solitary place; and there He prayed" (Mark 1:35). Daniel prayed regularly before challenges and crises arose. When he was faced with crises, his default was not fear and anxiety, but prayer to the One who was and is able to do all things.

Mary, Queen of Scots was quoted to have said, "I fear the prayers of John Knox more than all the assembled armies of Europe". Prayer touches heaven and changes earth! "If my people who are called by name, shall humble themselves and PRAY and seek my face…heal their land" (2 Chron. 7:14). I encourage you today to make prayer a lifestyle. Develop a schedule for prayer. Let prayer be the "as usual" thing to do. Whether you are fixing breakfast for the family… PRAY, while driving to work… PRAY, during your lunch break… PRAY, while in the shower…PRAY, on the flight…PRAY, while knitting…PRAY, in the car wash…PRAY, while tending your garden…PRAY. The list goes on. Things change when we pray. Dwight L. Moody said, "Every great movement of God can be traced to a kneeling figure." It will amaze you what God will do with your prayers.
Stanley Appiah

paragraphs: In Daniel 7:15-22, we read about the interpretation of Daniel’s dream as he had a desire to know its meaning. Looking at Daniel’s experience, we can learn what steps to take when we have a significant dream or vision and don’t understand its meaning, especially if it’s somewhat frightening and mysterious. For clarification, a dream is experienced while sleeping whereas a vision is experienced while awake.

The first thing Daniel did was discern the source. In verse sixteen, we read that there was a man standing there so Daniel asked him the meaning of all this. I believe Daniel knew in his spirit that the dream was from God and the man standing there was no doubt an angel. My experience with my own dreams is that I am aware of a dream being from God versus one that is from what I am experiencing in my day-to-day life. If I’m not sure of the source, I ask God, “Is this dream from you?” Just as Daniel turned to the man standing there, it is always wise to ask or share with someone you trust for spiritual insight, such as a pastor or a mentor. We need not fear or dismiss dreams as they are one of the forms of communication God uses to speak to us. The Bible consistently reveals God speaking to people in dreams, both in the Old Testament and New Testament. Dreams may be used as a warning, confirmation or be prophetic in nature.

The second thing Daniel did was record his dream (Dan. 7:1). When you have a dream, write it down as soon as possible while details are still fresh in your mind. Do not go back to sleep and then try to remember your dream in the morning because the details will not be as clear.

The third thing Daniel did was seek the help of God. Earlier in Daniel 2:27-28, King Nebuchadnezzar demanded that all his wise men interpret his dream. Daniel goes home, gathers his friends, prays and asks God for help. His response to the king was that there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries. In Genesis 40:8, Joseph said, "Do not interpretations belong to God?"

It’s not up to us to interpret our dreams, but to allow God to reveal it in his time. God does not give us a dream and then expect us to figure it out ourselves. God does not give us dreams to confuse us or to cause us to be fearful because He is not the author of confusion (1 Cor. 14:33).

The fourth thing Daniel did was to wait upon God. In Daniel 7, God reveals the meaning of the dream immediately, but later Daniel has a vision and it’s twenty-one days before he receives an answer (Dan. 10:12-13). The angel came to respond to Daniel immediately when he asked, but faced resistance by the enemy for twenty-one days. God is sovereign and nothing happens outside of his plan and his timing. He knows all things and is in complete control and has the power to carry it out.

As humans we tend to be impatient and want to know everything now. Waiting can seem like an eternity, but we need to wait for God to reveal things to us in His time. The answer might come to us immediately, in a couple of months or even a number of years. As I’ve grown older, my experiences have taught me to be patient and wait, knowing that God is faithful and will show me in His timing.
Jim Stroh

paragraphs: Do you struggle to pray passionately? Too often, amidst the difficulty of finding time to pray, we also face the challenge of having the strength to pray with passion. We are more prone to pray from a place of exhaustion rather than with energy. There could be several reasons why this can happen, but through Daniel’s life, we learn that passionate prayers to God are encouraged and needed. We need to first know what is fueling him to pray this way. In Daniel 9:2-3, we see that Daniel began to pray after understanding from the scriptures the word of the Lord that came to Jeremiah regarding the desolate sanctuary.

This is the foundation of Daniel’s passionate prayers; he read God’s word which revealed to him God’s plan for his people and it inspired him to pray passionately. If we want to pray passionately, we need faith to fuel it. To generate faith, we need to first read and understand God’s written Word. The passion of our prayers must be inspired by the revelation of God’s Word. In Psalm 119:28, it says, "My soul is weary with sorrow; strengthen me according to Your word."

David here tells us that our soul is strengthened according to God’s Word. To pray with passion, we need our souls to be strong first. God’s Word has the power to strengthen our souls by enlightening our minds and comforting our hearts with the truth, which causes us to respond in humility and dependency on God. In Matthew 4:4, Jesus affirms this truth by quoting Deuteronomy 8:3: "Man does not live on bread alone but on every word that comes from the mouth of God." As human beings, we don’t live by physical food alone, but by the words that come from God’s mouth. If we consistently read and meditate on God’s Word, our faith will increase and no matter how physically tired we might be, the Word of God causes us to pray.

As we read more of God’s Word, we recognize his character and capabilities. In Daniel 9:17, we see that Daniel begins by addressing God as the one who hears prayers and petitions. He acknowledges God’s greatness, faithfulness and mercy. This sets the foundation for his requests, reminding us to approach God with reverence and an awareness of His attributes. To gain this understanding of God, Daniel had to read the scriptures that revealed who God is. When we read our Bibles, do we take a moment to ponder about what the verse is saying about God? Does it humble us to know that He is greater than us and has the power to act?

At the heart of Daniel’s passionate prayer, he recognizes God’s sovereignty and righteousness over all things and he appeals to this attribute of God in humility. In verse eighteen, we see the reason for his requests are not based on his own righteousness, but on God’s mercy. From where did he get this understanding of God? From reading the scriptures! Based on this revelation of God, he passionately appeals for God’s attention, forgiveness and deliverance for God’s people. Daniel is convinced that there is no one else who can address the problems that the people of God are facing except God alone
In addition to humbling himself before God, we see that his passionate prayer shows his desperation for God.
"Look with favour" (vs.17)
"Give ear" (vs.18)
"Open Your eyes" (vs.18)
"Lord, listen!" (vs.19)
"Lord, forgive!" (vs.19)
"Lord, hear and act!" (vs.19)
"Do not delay" (vs.19)

All these phrases are passionate expressions that identify the need to pray. Daniel does not distance himself from the situation of the desolate sanctuary. He is inspired by God’s Word to pray. Passionate prayers involve a personal identification with the needs we bring before God, acknowledging our dependency on His grace. It will sound persistent, urgent and desperate. He implores God to hear, see, forgive and act without delay. Now when he prays like this, does it mean God doesn’t see, hear or know everything going on? No, it does not! Why pray as though God has his eyes and ears closed and is delaying to act? Bold and unashamed faith. His passionate prayer is marked by a fervent desire for God to move swiftly in response to his cries.

As we reflect on Daniel’s passionate prayer, we are invited to examine our own. Are our prayers passionate? Are we humble before God and desperate for Him to act on our needs? If not, we need to assess ourselves to see if we are worn down and distracted. If we are, when was the last time we spent time in God’s written Word to strengthen our souls with faith? That is the secret to passionate prayer!
Pastor Joshua Mathew

paragraphs: Daniel 11 is considered by some scholars to be the most detailed prophecy in the Bible. It demonstrates once more the omniscience and sovereignty of God over world events. The content of this biblical prophecy matches so accurately with historical events that it has led some people to believe that it was not written during Daniel’s lifetime, but as the Lord says in Isaiah 46:10a, "I make known the end from the beginning, from ancient times, what is still to come." Therefore, the prophetic agreement with historical events proves that the prophecy came from the Lord (Deut. 18:21-22).

God sent an angel to Daniel to unveil a series of geopolitical events set to unfold in the future in two of Israel’s neighbouring nations. These events are often associated with the Ptolemies in Egypt and the Seleucids in Syria, known as the Kings of the South and the North. Their alliances and conflicts had a profound impact on the people of Israel, with the stronger of the two often exerting control over Israel. The Ptolemies and the Seleucids were part of the Diadochi, the Successors of Alexander the Great, king of Greece. After Alexander’s demise, his kingdom was divided into four, two established in Egypt and Syria. To grasp the context of Daniel 11:14-28, we must delve into the historical events that commenced in Daniel 11:5.

The king of the South, Ptolemy I Soter, one of the successors of Alexander the Great, laid the foundation of the Ptolemy dynasty in Egypt. Seleucus I Nicator, a former Greek commander who had sought refuge in Egypt, became his subordinate. Later, Seleucus I Nicator returned to Babylon and established a kingdom that surpassed the strength of his former master, as prophesied in Daniel 11:5. Thus, the Seleucid dynasty was born. The subsequent verses delve into how their descendants, through wars, intrigue, deceit, flattery, arranged marriage and taxes would strive to maintain control over their territories. The people of Israel, caught in the crossfire, were at the mercy of the ruling power (Dan. 11:14 & 11:16). In particular, a "contemptible person," as Daniel 11:21 describes, would have "his heart set against the holy covenant."  Scholars believe this person is the notorious Antiochus IV Epiphanes from the Seleucid dynasty, infamous for desecrating the temple and setting up the abomination that causes desolation (Dan. 11:31).

Fast forward more than 2500 years after the events of our devotional today, what can we, as New Testament believers, learn from it? Quite a lot! First, we start with the fact that God is faithful. We now know that despite Israel being at the mercy of the Ptolemies and the Seleucids for nearly 200 years, God eventually delivered them, putting an end to both dynasties. Second, we are reminded that God’s Word never fails; what He decrees comes to pass. Thus, we are confident that the Old and New Testament's unfulfilled prophecies will each come to pass, amongst which is the second coming of Christ to which we pray: Maranatha! Last, we see through the narrative of today’s scripture the desire of God to reveal to His people what is yet to come (Matt. 24:25). Therefore, as Daniel set his heart to know about the fate of His people, let us earnestly seek the Lord to give us a prophetic discernment about the issues of our times (Jl. 2:28-29).
Estelle Inack
